articles.title: Bridging the Gap: How CS + MBA Thinking Transforms Project Delivery
articles.summary: Why technical fluency and business psychology are a superpower for Technical Project Managers navigating tight deadlines and stakeholder expectations.
articles.content:
Bridging the Gap: How CS + MBA Thinking Transforms Project Delivery

Over the years, I have noticed that some of the hardest project problems are not really technical problems.

They might look like one at first. A delayed integration. A changing requirement. A development estimate that suddenly gets bigger. A client asking why something that looks simple is taking so long.

But when you dig a little deeper, there is usually something else going on.

Sometimes the requirement was never properly understood. Sometimes the business expectation and the technical reality were not aligned. Sometimes the team is solving the wrong problem very efficiently.

This is probably one of the biggest reasons I have come to value having a background in both Computer Science and Business Administration.

My Computer Science background taught me how software and systems work. My MBA taught me to look at decisions through the lens of business, people, cost, risk and outcomes. Project management sits somewhere in between those two worlds.

And working in that middle ground has changed the way I approach delivery.

Learning to See the Same Project From Two Sides

When I started working more closely with software teams, I gradually realised that the same project can look completely different depending on where you are standing.

A developer may look at a requirement and immediately see database changes, API dependencies, edge cases, testing and deployment considerations.

A client may see a button on a screen and wonder why it cannot simply be added.

Neither person is necessarily wrong.

There is just a gap between what the requirement looks like and what it actually takes to deliver.

Having a technical background helps me understand that gap. I do not need to write the implementation myself, and I don't try to interfere with an engineer's job. But I can understand enough of the technical discussion to recognise when a seemingly small request has wider implications.

That becomes especially useful during estimation.

A feature that sounds like a two-day task during a client call can turn into a much larger piece of work once authentication, existing data, third-party integrations, testing and deployment are considered.

Being able to recognise that early makes conversations with both the client and the team much easier.

Then There Is the Other Question: Why?

This is where my business education has probably influenced my project management style the most.

Technical teams naturally think about how something should be built.

Business stakeholders usually care more about why it needs to be built and what they will get from it.

As a project manager, I have to care about both.

I have worked on projects where a requested feature initially appeared to be an obvious priority. But after discussing the requirement in more detail, it became clear that the real business problem was slightly different.

That changes the conversation.

Instead of simply asking the team to build exactly what was requested, I can ask what outcome the client is actually looking for and then discuss whether the proposed solution is the best way to reach it.

It does not mean saying no to clients.

It means making sure that we are not confusing a requested solution with the actual requirement.

Managing Multiple Projects Taught Me Something Else

One thing you learn fairly quickly when managing several projects is that you cannot treat every project in exactly the same way.

Over the course of my work, I have been involved with more than 27 projects across different sizes and requirements. At my busiest, I have had around 8 to 9 small to large projects moving through different stages at the same time.

That experience changed how I think about project control.

A project does not become manageable just because there is a project plan.

You need to know what is actually happening.

Which dependency is holding things up? Which decision is waiting for the client? Is the team genuinely behind schedule, or is the estimate changing because the scope changed? Is a technical issue actually a blocker, or can another part of the project continue?

When several projects are moving at once, these details start becoming important very quickly.

It also taught me that project management is not about constantly chasing people for updates.

If I have to repeatedly ask someone, "What's the status?", there may already be a problem with how the work is being tracked or communicated.

I would rather have a system where the important information is visible and the conversation is about decisions and blockers instead of simply collecting status updates.

Technical Understanding Makes Difficult Conversations Easier

One of the less obvious benefits of a CS background is that it makes technical conversations with clients easier.

There have been plenty of situations where a client has raised a concern that initially sounds like a technical issue but is actually a question about business impact.

For example, they may not really care about the underlying architecture. They care about whether a delay will affect their launch date.

So instead of explaining the technical problem in excessive detail, I try to connect it to what matters to them.

If an integration is blocked because another component is not ready, the useful conversation is not necessarily about the internal architecture. It is about what this means for the delivery timeline, what can continue in parallel and what decision needs to be made.

That translation between technical detail and business consequence is a surprisingly important part of project management.

Sometimes the Best Decision Is to Challenge the Plan

There is also a misconception that a project manager's job is to keep everyone moving according to the original plan.

I don't think that is always true.

A plan is created using the information available at the time. Projects change. Requirements change. Priorities change. Sometimes we learn something halfway through a project that we simply did not know at the beginning.

Holding onto the original plan just because it was the original plan is not necessarily good project management.

Sometimes the right thing is to revisit the scope.

Sometimes it is to change the sequence of work.

Sometimes it means telling a stakeholder that adding another requirement now will have consequences for the timeline.

And occasionally, it means admitting that the original approach was not the best one.

I think having both technical and business perspectives helps here because you can look at the consequences from more than one angle.

The Human Side Still Matters Most

For all the value that technical knowledge and business education bring, projects are still delivered by people.

A technically sound plan can fall apart because communication is poor. A highly capable developer can become frustrated because priorities keep changing. A client can lose confidence simply because they do not know what is happening.

Managing those situations requires more than frameworks and project management terminology.

It requires listening.

Sometimes the most useful thing I can do in a meeting is let people explain what is actually bothering them before trying to solve it.

There have been situations where what initially appeared to be a scheduling problem turned out to be a communication problem. There have also been cases where a team seemed to be moving slowly when the real issue was an unclear requirement.

You don't always find those things in a project tracker.

What CS + MBA Has Changed for Me

If I had to summarise the value of having both backgrounds, I would not say that it makes me better at everything.

It simply gives me two different lenses.

Computer Science helps me understand the mechanics.

How systems interact. Where dependencies might exist. Why something that looks simple may not actually be simple.

An MBA helps me understand the context.

What the business is trying to achieve. Where the value is. What the risks and trade-offs look like. Why a particular priority matters.

Project management is where I bring those perspectives together.

When I look at a project today, I am not only thinking about whether the team can deliver the requirement.

I am also thinking about whether we understand the requirement correctly, whether it solves the right problem, whether the timeline makes sense, what risks are sitting underneath it and whether everyone involved has the same expectation of what "done" actually means.

Delivery Is More Than Getting Things Done

After managing projects across different scales, I have become less interested in the idea of simply keeping a project "on track".

Being on track only matters if you are heading in the right direction.

A project delivered exactly according to an outdated plan is not necessarily a successful project.

For me, good project delivery is about creating that connection between technology, business and people.

The technology has to work.

The business case has to make sense.

The team needs enough clarity to do good work.

The client needs confidence in what is being delivered.

And when something changes, the project needs to be able to respond without losing sight of the outcome.

That is probably the biggest lesson I have taken from working at the intersection of technology and business.

Computer Science taught me how to understand the solution.

Business taught me to question the value behind it.

Project management taught me how to bring the two together and actually get it delivered.

recommendations.text: I’ve had the privilege of working under Fazal Mahmud Hasan for over a year as a Business Analyst, and I continue to do so. Throughout this time, I’ve learned a great deal from him about project management — especially when it comes to handling multiple SaaS, ERP, and AI-based projects with precision and clarity.  He brings an exceptional balance of technical expertise and leadership to every project. He has a unique ability to keep complex workflows organized while maintaining a collaborative environment where every team member feels valued and guided.  Working with him has been an inspiring experience that’s helped me grow both professionally and personally. His mentorship has had a lasting impact on how I approach project management.

recommendations.author: Mushfiqur Rahman
recommendations.headline: Software Engineer III (AI/ML)
recommendations.text: I’ve had the pleasure of working closely with Fazal Mahmud Hassan, and I can confidently say he is one of the most well-rounded Technical Project Managers I have met. He leads with empathy and always shows genuine care for his team, creating a supportive and motivating work environment that brings out the best in everyone.  Fazal bhai’s technical expertise is exceptional. His deep knowledge of computers, hardware, and automation makes him the go-to person whenever something complex comes up. He has a rare ability to simplify technical challenges and guide the team toward effective solutions.  In meetings, Fazal bhai is the one who steps up when alignment is needed. He takes charge with clarity and confidence, ensuring that discussions are productive and clients are always on the same page. His positive attitude and great sense of humor make every interaction enjoyable and energizing.  Beyond work, Fazal bhai’s values truly stand out. He maintains strong family ties and approaches both personal and professional life with optimism and forward thinking. His passion for personal projects, especially in automation, shows how deeply he loves technology and how eager he is to share that enthusiasm with others.  Working with Fazal bhai is both inspiring and rewarding. He brings technical depth, leadership, and positivity to every situation, and I feel lucky to have had the opportunity to collaborate with him.
